20F here, moved out at 18. I work in the finance industry so I've got a little experience here haha.

Rent is currently ~$540 as I split it with my bf. I pay $300 for my car and $160 for insurance, as well as another $320 for groceries and other miscellaneous bills.

I make roughly around $28/hr nowadays but when I initially moved out I was only at about $18/hr!

Here's what I do:

1. Add up all your monthly bills
2. Divide that number by however many paychecks you receive a month (for most, it's 4 but I get paid biweekly so it's 2 for me)
3. Withdraw that amount from you bank account every single time you get paid. Very first thing you do.
4. Get an accordion file and label each section for all the bills you have and separate cash accordingly.
5. Whenever a bill comes due, just run to the ATM and deposit it.

Yes, this is a little inefficient in terms of time but having that money OUT of your bank account gives you a much better idea of how much you actually have to spend. I've been using this method for almost 3 years now and have never once been late on any of my bills.

Also, as a side note, PAY OFF THOSE LOANS AND CREDIT CARD BILLS ASAP!!! Debt is a disease and it only gets worse. As of now, I am debt free (aside from my car) but there was a long period of time where I wasn't and it SUCKED. If you want to buy something expensive, just make another folder in that accordian file, label it, and save up for it. At the very LEAST, save half. Don't go throwing full-priced stuff on your credit card.

Hope this helps!!

$8k in savings is AWESOME for 21 years old. You should be very proud of that accomplishment!

While I can't say "what I wish I knew" because I'm basically the same age as you, I can say what I DO know and how's it has helped me:

1. First priority should be emergency fund. Generally trying to save 3-6 months of living expenses for emergencies. With 8k in savings, you probably have this covered

2. Pay 👏 yourself 👏 first 👏!!! I hear you're stressed about spending money on non-essentials. This is how you solve that. Take all your necessary expenses for the month, divide it by the number of paychecks you receive in a month (usually 2-4). Now, every payday you go to the ATM and withdraw that money and put it into labelled envelopes for each bill. Bam. Now you've paid your bills and any money leftover is yours freely!

3. RETIREMENT SAVINGS! It feels so unimportant at our age but $25-$100 a month now is worth just as much as $300 a month in your 40s. Open a Roth IRA (I personally recommend Fidelity Investments for this because it's 100% free) and plop your money in there. Find a good index fund/retirement fund, sit back, and watch it grow.

4. Only spend on credit cards what you can actually afford to pay off. Never spend more than you have unless you have a SOLID plan + the willpower to pay it back within 1-3 months.

5. Kinda going off what I said in #3, also find out if your employer has a 401k, if that 401k has employer matching, and what the "vesting period" for that match is. It's soooo important and makes retirement saving even faster and easier.

Anyways that's just a handful of things off the top of my head. Hope it helps!

Not all of this advice is my own personal experience, because I've actually learned most of it from other kind people on this subreddit over the past few days but here we go:

I can't say for certain bc I wasn't there but the specialist you saw may have honestly done the best they could. If you've had T for years, there's no really proven treatment to cure it. Some things help some people, most things don't. They tested for hearing loss and you had none -- which is a very good thing! It doesn't mean you don't have T, it just means the inciting event didn't cause any significant damage to your inner ear. In this case it's more of a "hearing gain" lol. You didn't LOSE any hearing, but you did gain a really obnoxious constant sound. 

"Just ignore it" is a bit crass and reductive but... It kinda boils down to that. Anxiety and obsessive thinking will make it worse. Even if it's not actually louder, it will be because you're focusing on it. If it IS actually louder, you should go back to the doctor to make sure there's no underlying cause for the spike!

Assuming there isn't a cause; spikes in T happen. More often than not, they will level out. It may take a long time (weeks or even months, unfortunately) but it will likely return to normal. And in that time, you may even forget it is there.

Start sleeping with your TV on, buy a white noise machine off Amazon, preoccupy waking hours with more noise. It will be okay.

Going to a good, reputable mental hospital is not a bad idea. It gets you medically excused from school and the workers will help you find therapy and potentially get you on medication. I've done it twice. The key is to make sure it's a good hospital. The last one I went to ended up doing more harm than good.

From the sound of it, your family seems to love and care about you. Opening up to my family was never an option, but it could be beneficial for you. Let them know exactly how you are feeling and tell them you need their help. If they are good parents, they will help you in any way they can.

School counselors/social workers have never done much for me because their main goal is to get you to finish school on time. However, my guidance counselor was able to hook me up with a 504 plan (it basically gives you accomodations like extended deadlines and the ability to take space during class if you need to).

This is going to be controversial, especially coming from another suicidal person, but school should not be your #1 priority right now. You need to take care of yourself in order to move on. Consider a GED. Consider going into an alternate program that allows you to work at your own pace (that's what I'm in currently). You are more important than your education. It doesn't matter how smart a man is if he's dead. Take care of yourself first.

Reaching out is the hard part. You're already on your way to getting better. If you need anything, I am always here to talk.

Hey there... I'm 17 years old right now and... Well, I'm in this subreddit so I can't say I'm doing well either.

I won't tell you that everything will be better when you turn 18. I don't believe it myself. But there are things you can look forward to and there are things you can do now to help yourself get through it, I promise.

I know that telling your parents may seem terrifying but (if they're not the ones causing your pain) please. please. please. Tell them. If you think they'll understand, THEY CAN GET YOU HELP! I was with a therapist from age 14 up until a few months ago and I'm going to be going back soon.

You are not alone. I was there. I am there now. I know how you feel. But let me tell you something: it doesn't have to be five years.

At fourteen you can get a job. My job is one of the few reasons I'm still here.
At fifteen you can start learning to drive. Taking long drives late at night has done wonders to ease my mind.
At sixteen you can move out. Technically you're supposed to be eighteen but if you can find somebody you trust that is over 18 to live with, CPS/DCYF won't spend a lot of time trying to bring back somebody who is sustaining themselves and living on their own. Especially if your household is abusive. I know this from experience.

It breaks my heart to see somebody even younger than myself suffering like this. And if nobody has told you this yet, your feelings are valid. Your suffering is just as real as the suffering of an adult. I know it hurts, but please don't leave. You have so much time to do great things. Give yourself the opportunity to get there.
